findings.title: Do not execute unpinned remote script during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads arbitrary code over the network and executes it as root inside the image with no version pin, checksum, or signature verification. The build is non-reproducible and any compromise/change of the remote host (or its DNS/TLS chain) becomes code execution baked into every produced image. Additionally, `-sL` lacks `-f`, so an HTTP 404/500 response body is still piped into `sh` and curl's exit status is discarded because the pipeline status is `sh`'s, meaning download failures are silently fed to the shell rather than aborting the build.

findings.title: Don't swallow Load's error in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards Load's error via `v, _ := Load(key, m)` and returns the zero value "". Callers can no longer distinguish a missing key (Load returns ErrMissing with "", src/store.go:9-11) from a key that is legitimately present with an empty-string value, and any non-ErrMissing error Load may return in the future is likewise reported as a real value. Because the function is exported, every downstream consumer is forced to treat failure as data, and a caller that persists/branches on the result cannot detect the missing/failed case.

findings.title: Run now returns before results are sent, enabling send on closed channel
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation blocked until every result was written, so a caller could safely `for j := range jobs { ... }; close(results)` after Run returned. The new goroutine-per-job form makes Run return immediately while the sends happen later on unrelated goroutines. A caller that closes `results` right after Run returns (the previous, now-broken usage pattern) triggers `panic: send on closed channel`, or silently drops in-flight results. Completion is no longer observable, so the function's delivery contract is gone.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord OR-widening allows non-admin same-tenant and cross-tenant admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required both `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. The new `||` returns true in two previously-forbidden cases: (1) a non-admin whose `tenantId` matches the record — e.g. session {isAdmin:false, tenantId:'t1'} vs record {tenantId:'t1'} now yields true, granting an ordinary user destructive delete rights; (2) an admin with a mismatched tenant — session {isAdmin:true, tenantId:'t1'} vs record {tenantId:'t2'} also yields true. Every caller of this predicate therefore permits deletes it was designed to reject, which is a privilege-escalation/data-loss path via an exported authorization helper.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows all errors, causing silent settings reset
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, malformed JSON or a missing/wrong-typed field threw ('bad theme'/'bad fontSize'), so updateFontSize aborted and never wrote. The new catch turns every failure into a valid-looking Settings equal to DEFAULTS. updateFontSize (line 20) calls parseSettings, cannot tell the result is a fallback, sets fontSize on it, and saves it — so a corrupt/legacy raw value now silently overwrites the user's stored theme with 'light' (and resets other fields) instead of surfacing the error. This is silent data loss / error-signal downgrade on an existing live path.

findings.title: pageCount floors, dropping the final partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount is the exported public contract for the number of pages holding totalItems at pageSize. Math.floor(totalItems / pageSize) returns 2 for totalItems=5,pageSize=2 even though items 5 occupies a third page, and returns 0 for totalItems=1,pageSize=10 while one item exists. Every consumer that sizes a page list/loop from this value omits the trailing page, so those records are never fetched or rendered (silent data loss at the caller). The base implementation (Math.ceil) was correct and this PR regresses it; there is no caller in-repo whose intent would justify flooring.

facts.meaning: The page count rounds down instead of up.
A remainder/partial final page is omitted or a small result becomes zero pages.

findings.title: buildReport decouples artifacts from requested branch via hardcoded ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change artifacts came from `commit = build.ref(branch)`, so `builtFrom` and `artifacts` described the same commit. Now `artifacts` comes from `build.ref("verified")` (line 13) while `builtFrom` still reports the branch commit (line 12). For any caller passing a branch other than whatever "verified" resolves to, the returned BuildReport lists artifacts that do not correspond to the stated `builtFrom` commit; the `branch` argument no longer influences `artifacts` at all. "verified" is also a hardcoded magic ref name that need not exist in the caller's Build, in which case `ref` yields an unresolved value that is fed straight into `artifactsAt`.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores `limit` and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment at src/feed.ts:1 promises 'Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first', and the previous body enforced it with `.slice(0, limit)`. The new body returns the full reversed copy `sorted` for any limit > 0, so the cap is silently lost. renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) calls recentEntries(all, 20) and copies `page` into a 20-slot array assuming it holds at most 20 items; with the cap removed, `page.length` is `all.length`, so the loop at src/feed.ts:11 writes indices 20..all.length-1 and renderFeed returns an unbounded, oversized feed instead of a 20-item page.

findings.title: Keep entry-count in sync with the filtered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The change filters `rows` down to `live` (non-stale entries) but leaves the header computed from `entries.length` (`headerLines(opts, entries.length)` @src/manifest.ts:22 -> `# entry-count: ${count}` @src/manifest.ts:15). Rendering [{stale:false},{stale:true}] now emits `# entry-count: 2` above a single data row, so the manifest is internally inconsistent: the declared count no longer equals the number of entries actually serialized. Any consumer that parses the manifest and trusts `entry-count` (to size a buffer, validate completeness, or detect truncation) gets an off-by-k result whenever any entry is stale; previously count exactly equaled the row count.

findings.title: Restore execute(); it now always throws instead of returning a result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute() previously returned input.toUpperCase(). It is an exported, public function (the only function in the repo's single source file), so every consumer that calls it now gets an uncaught Error on every invocation; the function has no non-throwing path and the unchanged signature still declares `: string`.

findings.title: Viewer check in isEligible over-blocks read-only path in handle()
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() gates its distinguished viewer outcome behind isEligible: `if (!isEligible(req)) return "rejected"` (line 24) runs BEFORE `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only"` (line 25). Adding `if (req.role === "viewer") return false` to isEligible (line 18) means every active viewer now fails eligibility and handle() returns "rejected" instead of "read-only". Viewer's read-only handling is an independently approvable action the eligibility predicate should not govern, and line 25 is now unreachable dead code. Previously (base a84a4e8) an active viewer with attempts < 5 returned "read-only".

findings.title: Requiring paid payment blocks saveDraft for unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate. Adding `&& order.payment === "paid"` makes it return false for payment === "missing" (branch taken: `payment === "paid"` is false → whole expression false). saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) calls the same shared predicate, so saving a draft of an unpaid order now returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Saving a draft is legitimately approvable without payment, so this is an over-block on a live path.

findings.title: Snapshot files taken from `stable`, not the recorded commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `files` was computed from `head` (the head commit of the requested `channel`), so the returned Snapshot was internally consistent: `commit === filesAt` argument. The diff adds `const stable = repo.headCommit("stable")` (line 14) and switches the file list to `repo.filesAt(stable)` (line 18), while `commit` still comes from `repo.headCommit(channel)` (line 13) and `channel` is still the caller-supplied value (line 17). The result is a torn snapshot: for any channel other than `stable`, `commit` does not correspond to the revision the `files` array was read from. Consumers that render/upload `files` for the recorded `commit` receive the wrong revision's contents, and `channel` mislabels which revision was actually captured. It also introduces a hard dependency on a branch literally named `stable`, which may not exist for the requested repo and can now fail or return a divergent revision unrelated to `channel`.

findings.title: apply_values mutates caller DataFrame in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Base body did `result = df.copy()` then assigned into `result`, leaving the caller's `df` untouched. The new body writes directly into the caller's frame with `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` and returns that same object. Any caller that reads or reuses its `df` after the call (applying a second mapping, comparing pre/post state, logging the input, or holding a shared reference) now observes mutated values — a silent in-place corruption of caller data.

findings.title: Restore CI workflow: rename to docs/ci.md disables all CI
findings.whyItBreaks: The 100%-similarity rename moves the workflow from `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to `docs/ci.md`. GitHub Actions only discovers workflow definitions under `.github/workflows/` with a `.yml`/`.yaml` extension, so the guard that loads workflows rejects this new path/extension: no push or pull_request event will ever trigger the lint/test job again. Verified `git ls-files` at HEAD contains no `.github/**` at all and `git show base:.github/workflows/ci.yml` held the `on: push/pull_request` + `npm run lint`/`npm test` job that disappears. This is a broken workflow, and it contradicts the unchanged README line 5 ('CI runs lint and tests on every push'), so merges proceed with no lint/test gate.

findings.title: Remove dbg!(items): it moves items and breaks compilation
findings.whyItBreaks: std::dbg! takes ownership of a non-Copy expression (documented: "Invoking the macro on an expression moves and takes ownership of it"). `dbg!(items)` therefore moves the Vec<String> into the macro and drops it at the end of the statement, so the subsequent `items.len()` on line 3 reads a moved value and the crate fails to compile with E0382 (borrow of moved value: `items`). Separately, dbg! emits the entire owned value to stderr and behaves identically in release builds, so shipping it also leaks item contents/pollutes output.

findings.title: changedPaths no longer computed against fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface documents fromRevision as 'Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision.' The diff adds `const latest = store.resolve("latest")` and passes `latest` to readChangedPaths, so the returned paths describe the diff from latest while the object still advertises fromRevision = store.resolve(pinnedTag). Any consumer that replays changedPaths on top of fromRevision (as the contract instructs) applies paths derived from a different base, producing a wrong file set (missing/extra changes) rather than the intended pinned changeset.

findings.title: Rename contact_email breaks existing query selecting email
findings.whyItBreaks: This migration renames users.email to users.contact_email, but the repository's only consumer of that column, src/query.sql:1 (`SELECT email FROM users;`), is not updated in this change. After 0002_rename.sql applies, that query references a column that no longer exists, so any code path executing it errors out (unknown column 'email') and returns no user data. Substituting the renamed value into the read path: column=email->contact_email -> src/query.sql:1 SELECT email FROM users -> resolves against new schema -> column not found -> runtime failure.

findings.title: Remove hardcoded live billing API key from source
findings.whyItBreaks: A constant `bk_live_...` credential is now committed in the module and returned to every caller via makeClient(). Anyone with repository read access (or a downstream fork/artifact bundle) obtains a usable live billing key, and it can never be rotated per-environment because it is baked into source. This is a directly exploitable credential leak, not a stylistic concern.

findings.title: Non-admins can now purge archived projects (authz bypass)
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, delete happened only on `user.isAdmin && project.archived`; every other case returned "forbidden". The new guards are independent: `user.isAdmin` is checked first and rejects admins, so a caller with isAdmin=false and archived=true falls through to `db.delete(project.id)` and gets "purged". The admin-only precondition was dropped, so a non-admin now destroys archived project data — an authorization bypass and data-loss path.

findings.title: Admin users are now rejected from purging archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden";` rejects exactly the actor the function is meant to authorize. An admin purging an archived project (the legitimate, previously-working action) now receives "forbidden" and no delete occurs — a user-facing regression for the only role permitted to perform the operation.

facts.meaning: The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.
Non-administrators can reach the destructive project purge/delete path.

findings.title: Restore missing-config fallback or startup crashes on absent file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() still returns None when the path does not exist (@app/config.py:7). The removed guard was the only code that turned that None into a default dict. Now startup() executes int(None["workers"]) and raises TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable instead of returning the prior default of 1 for a fresh/missing config file. Precondition substitution: settings=None (missing file) -> return int(settings["workers"]) @app/config.py:14 -> TypeError, blocking the startup entry point.

findings.title: Charge swallows gateway error and reports success
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, a gateway failure propagated as `fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)`; now the error is only logged and `Charge` unconditionally `return nil` (line 19). The exported function still advertises an `error` result, so every caller logically branches on it, but failure is now indistinguishable from success. Any caller that fulfills, persists, or bills on a nil result acts on a charge that never succeeded. This is a present defect in the public contract even with no in-repo caller yet: the `error` return is the API, and it now lies.

findings.title: Tenant isolation bypass: cache key omits tenantId
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey() returns only `settings:${name}`, so cache.set/cache.get in settingsFor are keyed by name alone. The first tenant to request a given `name` populates the entry; any other tenant requesting the same `name` gets a cache hit and is returned the first tenant's value without calling store.fetch with its own tenantId. Tenant-scoped settings are served across tenant boundaries (a security/isolation bypass, not just a perf change). The old key `${tenantId}:${name}` prevented this.

findings.title: invalidate drops tenantId, breaking per-tenant invalidation
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature changed from invalidate(tenantId, name) to invalidate(name). Existing consumers calling invalidate(tenantId, name) either fail to compile (TS strict) or, in non-type-checked contexts, pass the tenantId as `name`, so cache.delete targets `settings:<tenantId>` and the intended (tenantId, name) entry is never removed — a stale/wrong cache entry survives invalidation. Published as an exported API this is a breaking contract change on upgrade.

findings.title: Serialize reserve: await opens check-then-act oversell race
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve now reads remaining (line 15), evaluates the `remaining <= 0` guard (line 16), then awaits `store.save` (line 17) before writing the decremented value (line 18). The base version did read-check-write in a single synchronous block with no interleaving point, so it was atomic under JS's single-threaded model. With the added await, two concurrent `reserve(sku)` calls for a SKU with remaining=1 both read 1, both pass the guard, both await, and both resolve true and persist 0, granting two reservations for one unit. This is a regression introduced by this change (an interleaving point was inserted where none existed).

findings.title: Convert retry.ts to ms or delays balloon 1000x to ~8.3h
findings.whyItBreaks: This line changes the exported `backoff()` unit contract from seconds to milliseconds: before, `Math.min(30, 2**attempt)` seconds (max 30s, callers multiplied by 1000); now it returns milliseconds directly (max 30_000ms). `src/net/poll.ts:4` was updated to drop the `* 1000`, but the other consumer `src/jobs/retry.ts:12` still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. Substituting the new value: attempt 0 -> 1_000ms*1000 = 1_000_000ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1_000ms; attempt>=5 -> 30_000ms*1000 = 30_000_000ms (~8.33 hours) per retry, versus the previous 30_000ms (30s) cap. Any job using `retry()` now stalls for minutes-to-hours between attempts, a user-facing workflow regression.

findings.title: Acknowledge file close error instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure). Base `store/save.go:24` returned `f.Close()` so any close-time failure (deferred write-back on NFS/SMB/CIFS, quota/ENOSPC surfacing at close, I/O error flushing the file descriptor) reached the caller of the exported `store.Save`. Head replaces that with `defer f.Close()` at store/save.go:13 and `return w.Flush()` at store/save.go:20, so the Close error is dropped and `Save` returns nil on a path where the write did not durably persist. `bufio.Writer.Flush` only pushes buffered bytes into the kernel via `write(2)`; it does not perform or report the fsync/close result, so a successful Flush is not evidence the close succeeded. Because `Save` is exported (public contract) with no in-repo callers, every eventual caller is forced to conflate 'close failed' with 'save succeeded' (distinguishable=no).

findings.title: Fix off-by-one: page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) range, but the loop iterates range(start, end - 1), excluding `end - 1` and therefore the final row of the window. The base version iterated range(start, end). Concretely, page_window(['a','b','c','d','e'], 0, 2) returned ['a','b'] before and now returns ['a']; for a last page that contains exactly one row (start == end - 1) the loop is empty and the page renders ''. Downstream, render_page() silently omits the dropped row and renumbers the remainder around the gap, and summarize() emits a page separator with an empty body, so displayed rows are lost and numbering becomes discontinuous for any page_size > 1.

findings.title: Restore correct TTL comparison in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was inverted. As written, `get` returns `entry.value` only when the entry has ALREADY exceeded the TTL (`Date.now() - storedAt > ttlMs`), and for a still-fresh entry it deletes the entry and returns null. Net effect: every lookup serves stale/expired data and evicts valid entries, so the cache is both wrong and useless. The original `Date.now() - entry.storedAt < this.ttlMs` was correct.

findings.title: Fix pruneDone skipping done jobs and mutating caller array
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array#forEach` iterates by index while `splice` re-indexes the array, so after removing a done job at index i the next job shifts into index i and is never inspected — consecutive done jobs are left in the result (e.g. `[{done:true},{done:true}]` returns one remaining done job). Additionally the function now mutates the caller's input array and returns that same reference, whereas the old `filter` returned a new array; any caller holding the original list has its job data silently mutated (dropped entries), which the previous contract did not do.

findings.title: busiest() mutates and reorders the caller's rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous code did `[...rows].sort(...)`, returning a sorted copy. The new `rows.sort(...)` calls Array.prototype.sort, which sorts the caller's array in place. Any caller that keeps using its `rows` array after calling busiest() — iterating it, displaying it, persisting it, passing it on — now sees elements permanently reordered by descending amount. The exported function silently corrupts caller-owned data, and re-calling other stats over the same array operates on a mutated input.

findings.title: averageAmount() returns NaN for empty rows after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting the `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard changes the exported function's empty-input behavior from the documented/previous value 0 to `0 / 0 === NaN`. NaN is a `number`, so it passes type checks and silently propagates: any consumer summing/averaging results, formatting them, or persisting them gets NaN instead of the prior 0 (and `averageAmount([]) === 0` becomes false), turning a legitimate 'no data' case into a poisoned value with no thrown error to detect.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparison in rankScores (default sort is lexicographic)
findings.whyItBreaks: `scores.sort()` sorts numbers as strings, then `reverse()`. For players [{score:2},{score:10}], n=1: sort() gives [10,2] ("10" < "2"), reverse gives [2,10], so cutoff=scores[0]=2; the filter keeps both and slice(0,1) returns the score-2 player. Base code (`sort((a,b)=>b-a)`) gave cutoff=10 and returned the score-10 player. Thus topPlayers/formatBoard report the wrong ordering and wrong winner for any score set where string order differs from numeric order (e.g. 9 vs 10, negatives, differing digit counts).

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() authenticates every inbound webhook: handle() calls it and returns 401 on mismatch vs 200 + processor(payload) on match (app/webhook.py:13-16). Python's `==` on str short-circuits at the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading bytes of the attacker-supplied given_signature match the real HMAC. An attacker can brute-force the signature byte-by-byte and, once it matches, have the webhook accepted as authentic (200 + processor executed), defeating the signature check. hmac.compare_digest exists precisely to make this comparison time-independent; the base revision used it and this change removes that protection.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so all three committed or rolled back together. After the change, only `_record_ledger` (line 23) runs inside the transaction; `_apply_balances` (line 24) runs after the transaction has exited/committed, and its two UPDATEs (lines 9-16) are themselves no longer wrapped in any transaction. If the debit succeeds and the credit UPDATE fails (constraint error, connection loss, crash), the source balance is reduced with no matching destination credit and no rollback — silent loss of funds. If any balance UPDATE fails before completing, the ledger already committed a transfer record, so ledger and balances permanently disagree and return `{"ok": True}` never executes while the recorded transfer appears to have happened.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, shifting billing-day boundaries by host TZ
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay() previously derived the day from UTC components (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate) and now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. The result is the host process timezone, not a canonical billing day: on a server at UTC-8, billingDay(new Date('2026-01-01T00:30:00Z')) changes from "2026-01-01" (base) to "2025-12-31" (head). Any timestamp whose UTC day differs from the host's local day is now bucketed into the wrong billing day, and the same instant yields different results on servers with different TZ settings — breaking determinism and cross-environment consistency of billing/usage attribution. sameBillingDay() at src/billing/day.ts:8 inherits the same shifted boundary, so day-equality/idempotency checks (e.g. de-duping two records near midnight) now disagree depending on the process timezone.

findings.title: Restore tenant in memo key; account-only key leaks cross-tenant profiles
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key lost its tenant scope. Two different tenants sharing an account name now map to the same key, so `cached` at src/profile.ts:15-16 is truthy for the wrong tenant and the first tenant's `Profile` is returned, skipping the `fetchProfile(tenant, account)` call at src/profile.ts:17. The returned `Profile` also carries the wrong `tenant`/`displayName` (src/profile.ts:1-5), turning a per-tenant lookup into a cross-tenant data disclosure, and the mis-hit is also persisted by `memo.set(key, profile)` at src/profile.ts:18.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error into indistinguishable empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, load() threw `missing: ${key}` when the key was absent, and that signal propagated through loadAll() (`keys.map((k) => load(k, store))`, src/store.ts:12). The added `catch { return "" }` (src/store.ts:6-7) discards that signal and returns "", which is a value Map<string,string> can legitimately hold. Every caller of load()/loadAll() is now forced to conflate 'key absent' with 'stored empty value', so a missing key silently yields "" instead of surfacing a failure — a public, exported path, so the unusable contract is the defect even absent external callers.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all failures and returns void
findings.whyItBreaks: Newly added exported retryBackground runs fn() in a try/catch, and on catch it just `continue`s; when config.retries is exhausted it falls through to an implicit `return` (void). A caller therefore cannot distinguish 'fn succeeded' from 'fn failed on every attempt' — total failure is reported as success. Because this is an exported public function, every eventual caller is forced to conflate the two, e.g. a caller that acks a task or clears a dirty flag after invoking it will do so even when nothing succeeded. The pre-existing retry() has the same catch/continue shape, but it predates this diff; the new public path ships the unusable contract now.

findings.title: Field renders 'len=undefined' / drops value for number inputs
findings.whyItBreaks: The type at line 2 was widened to `string | number`, but line 6 computes `value.length`. `number` has no `length`, so for any numeric value `value.length` is `undefined` and `label` becomes the literal string "len=undefined"; that string is then what `<input defaultValue>` renders. Even for string inputs the input no longer receives the caller's value at all (defaultValue was `value`, now it is the `len=<n>` label), a user-visible regression for every existing caller.

findings.title: Do not echo the TOKEN secret in the deploy workflow
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step injects secrets.TOKEN as an env var and interpolates it into a shell command (`echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`), so the credential is written to the Actions run log. GitHub log masking is best-effort (exact-match only; derived/transformed or multi-line values are not masked), and the token is additionally exported into the environment of a step that has no functional need for it. Anyone able to read build logs — collaborators, exported/archived logs, log-forwarding tooling — obtains the credential. The step also serves no deployment purpose (it does not pass the token to `make build`), so it is pure exposure.

findings.title: Restore 64 MiB maxBuffer on git() or large diffs fail the review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB (1024 * 1024). `git()` is used at line 140 to capture the full `git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>` patch. For any PR whose patch exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated code, large refactors) the child process is terminated with ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER, res.status is null so `res.status !== 0` at line 38 is true, and the helper throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty stderr. runGithub's catch (line 182) then posts a 'Needlefish: review failed' failing check and sets exitCode 1, so the review never runs. Before this diff the same call allowed 64 MiB, so this is a regression for previously-working large PRs. The neighboring gh()/ghText() helpers still pass maxBuffer, indicating the removal here was unintentional.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only` on codex exec so review runs cannot write
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns the codex CLI with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24) and feeds it an arbitrary prompt. The removed `-s read-only` was the only explicit sandbox confinement on that invocation; CLI flags override ambient `~/.codex/config.toml` sandbox_mode. After this change the spawned process instead inherits whatever sandbox mode the environment/configures by default or by config (e.g. `workspace-write` / `danger-full-access`), so a review run can now modify the repository under review, execute tooling, and (read-only mode also disables network) reach the network during what is supposed to be a non-mutating review.

findings.title: Diff from baseSha instead of merge-base pulls in non-PR changes
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is either an externally supplied PR base (env PR_BASE_SHA) or the fork point (fallback `git merge-base origin/main HEAD` at line 138) — the old code normalized both cases with `merge-base baseSha headSha` before diffing. Removing that normalization means that when PR_BASE_SHA is the base branch tip (the usual `github.event.pull_request.base.sha`) and HEAD is the PR head, `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot diff that also reports every change made on the base branch since the fork point, in reverse, as if the PR made them. The reviewer then reads/scores unrelated files, and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` (line 140) puts those files into changedPaths (line 141), which feeds inlineComments (line 58) — posting review comments on files/lines outside the PR diff, which GitHub rejects (422), failing the review run. This is exactly the precondition substitution: baseSha = base tip → `git diff baseSha HEAD` → unrelated paths in patch+changedFiles.

findings.title: String replace() re-interprets $&/$`/$' in bundle/patch, corrupting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the function replacer changes semantics: with a string replacement, patterns `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` are expanded by String.prototype.replace. `bundle.patch` is raw diff text and `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` embeds that same diff, and diffs of shell/sed/regex/template code routinely contain `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, or `$$`. `$&` expands to the matched placeholder (re-inserting `{{PATCH}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}`), `` $` `` expands to the entire preceding prompt, and `$'` to the entire following prompt — so the prompt handed to runCodex is silently duplicated/mangled rather than containing the literal patch. The base revision used `() => ...` precisely to avoid this.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review POST so reviews bind to reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: Head still computes and passes a specific reviewed revision (headSha = PR_HEAD_SHA || git rev-parse HEAD, src/adapters/github.ts:141) and the primary JSON path sends commit_id: headSha (src/adapters/github.ts:89). The changed fallback path (taken whenever the primary `--input -` POST throws, e.g. a 422 on inline comment positions) now omits commit_id, so GitHub defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the PR's current head (workflow_run / explicitly supplied SHA), or when a new commit lands while the review runs, the bot's REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT review — and the merge-blocking review state — is stamped on a revision that was never analyzed, and is inconsistent with the primary path's semantics.

findings.title: Restore throwing validation in normalizeFinding / normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously normalizeFinding THREW on malformed input (non-object, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-finite or <=0 lineStart/lineEnd) and normalizeReview defaulted to strict=true, propagating that throw to the caller. The new body never throws, and normalizeReview's `strict` parameter (previously default true) is removed, so every caller now receives a coerced value: severity "P9"->"P1", category "Bug"->"bug", missing file->"", lineStart "abc"->NaN (no Number.isFinite check remains), missing title->"Untitled finding". Failure is thus indistinguishable from a legitimate value at every decision point — a malformed model response that used to abort the review is now reported/persisted as a P1 finding on file="" line 0, corrupting whatever reports or scoring consumes the findings array.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in workflow_dispatch path
findings.whyItBreaks: This step (`Resolve PR refs`, workflow.yml:26) is the FIRST step of the job and runs before `actions/checkout` (workflow.yml:42), so on a clean runner there is no checked-out clone in $GITHUB_WORKSPACE and `gh` cannot infer the repository from a git remote. `-R "$REPO"` was the only thing supplying the repo target on the `workflow_dispatch` branch (pull_request events take the `EVENT_HEAD` branch and are unaffected). Without it `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` exits non-zero with an "unable to determine base repository" error; because the command is embedded in `echo "$(...)"` under the runner's default `bash -e`, the non-zero status is discarded and the step still exits 0, writing `head=` / `base=` empty to $GITHUB_OUTPUT. Downstream, `actions/checkout` with an empty `ref` falls back to the default ref (not the PR head) and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` are empty, so the manual-trigger review runs against the wrong revision instead of failing loudly. Note the local clone in this workspace has no git remotes at all (`git remote -v` prints nothing), which is exactly the condition under which the remote-free form fails.

findings.title: Restore validation so malformed review output is not silently defaulted
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change normalizeReview threw a distinct error for non-object input and for missing/non-string summary, missing/non-array findings, checked, or residual_risks. It is exported (the sole normalization entry point for model output -> RawReview) and the head body maps every one of those failure modes to the same value a legitimate clean review produces: summary "", findings [], checked [], residual_risks []. Any caller that derives a verdict from findings plus residual_risks now receives an empty review for garbage/parse-failed output and cannot distinguish it from a real 'no findings' review, so a false pass for unparsable output becomes possible. This is the exported-contract form of TRIGGER D: failure is coerced to a legitimate-looking value on the only public path, forcing every caller to conflate the two.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The job is still allowed to run on workflow_dispatch (line 24) and its required `pr_number` input is still consumed (line 47), but the step that resolved PR refs via `gh pr view` for non-pull_request events was deleted. On workflow_dispatch `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty, so the new expression `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` (line 29) falls back to `github.ref` — the branch the workflow was dispatched on (typically the default branch) — not the PR head. Likewise `github.event.pull_request.base.ref || 'main'` (line 35) fetches the default branch instead of the PR's real base, and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 45-46) are now empty strings where the removed `steps.refs.outputs.base/head` previously carried the real SHAs. Net effect on the documented manual-trigger path: the review runs against the wrong revision (and, if the PR's base is not `main`, the `git fetch origin refs/heads/$BASE_REF:...` step can fail outright and abort the job).

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync (large diffs now fail)
findings.whyItBreaks: This is the only helper used for `git diff <baseSha> HEAD` (src/adapters/local.ts:100), i.e. the full patch that is fed into the review bundle. Removing the explicit `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` reverts to Node's default of 1 MiB for spawnSync. When `git diff` output exceeds 1 MiB (common for lockfiles, generated files, vendored code, large refactors), the child is killed with ENOBUFS, `res.status` is null, and the guard at src/adapters/local.ts:12 throws. Since stderr is empty on ENOBUFS the user sees the opaque `git diff <base> HEAD failed: ` and never gets a review. Before this change the same repository reviewed fine up to 64 MiB, so this is a user-facing regression of the core path, not a style nit. Note the sibling `gh()` helper at src/adapters/local.ts:36 still keeps 64 MiB.

findings.title: Review-failure check downgraded to neutral — merge gate fails open
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch block for a failed `review(bundle)` (line 179-197), postCheck is now called with conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". GitHub evaluates required status checks as passing for `success`, `skipped`, and `neutral` (docs: about-protected-branches — "Required status checks must have a successful, skipped, or neutral status before collaborators can make changes"), whereas `failure` blocks merge. So when the reviewer errors out (LLM/API failure, malformed diff, etc.), a required "Needlefish" check now reports neutral and the PR becomes mergeable — previously it was blocked. The posted summary still asserts "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR", so the gate's own contract contradicts its conclusion. This is a fail-open on the error path: an error is mapped to the non-blocking default value and is no longer distinguishable from a legitimate pass at the merge decision point.

findings.title: Self-review lets a PR execute its own reviewer with a write token
findings.whyItBreaks: The trusted-tool checkout (frankekn/needlefish@main into path: needlefish) and absolute-path invocation were removed, and the review step now runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR head's own checkout. The job holds `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` and passes GH_TOKEN to that step (lines 55-59), the runner is self-hosted (line 23), and `pnpm install` (line 51) also executes the PR's dependency lifecycle scripts. A PR that edits src/ (or package.json) can therefore change the reviewer's verdict for its own PR and, more generally, run arbitrary PR-authored code with a token that can post reviews and fake passing checks. The `if:` gate only excludes fork PRs (`head.repo.full_name == github.repository`), so same-repo branches still take this path. The removed comment (base lines 3-6) stated this isolation is what 'prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool', so this is a deliberate security control being dropped rather than a neutral refactor.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently downgrades mis-cased/absent severity to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version normalized the raw value with `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before checking membership, so runtime inputs such as "p1", "p2" or " P0 " were canonicalized and preserved. The new code passes `raw.severity` straight to `SEVERITIES.includes(...)`, which only matches the exact upper-case literals, so any such value now fails the check and is replaced by the fallback. The fallback was also lowered from "P1" to "P3", so the same input that previously survived as P0/P1/P2 is now reported as the least-severe P3 (and an omitted severity, previously P1, is now P3). normalizeFinding consumes untyped JSON (normalizeReview takes `any` and maps `raw.findings`), where casing/whitespace is not guaranteed, so this is a real misclassification path, not a style nit.

findings.title: Restore GH token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, runCodex built a copied environment with GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN deleted and passed it via `env`, so the spawned `codex` CLI (and any process it in turn spawns, plus anything it forwards into model/tool context) could not see those credentials. Dropping the `env` option makes spawnSync inherit the full `process.env`, so the child now receives the reviewer's GitHub tokens verbatim. This is a credential-exposure regression on an exported function, not a cosmetic change: any live caller (this is public API; the file is the only source in-repo, but the function is the sole entry point for invoking codex) that runs in an environment holding these tokens now leaks them to a third-party binary.

findings.title: Restore fork guard so untrusted PR code can't run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` un-gates the job for PRs whose head repo is a fork (the job was previously skipped for forks). The job then checks out the contributor's commit (`ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, line 23), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, executes dependency lifecycle scripts) and runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) — all from the fork's branch — on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner (line 18) with `GH_TOKEN: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` exported (line 35) and declared `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` (lines 13-14). A fork contributor therefore gains arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted runner (host filesystem, network reach, and the token), enabling credential exfiltration or runner persistence.

findings.title: Explicit 0 duration is now silently replaced by the default
findings.whyItBreaks: `Number("0")` is finite but `0 > 0` is false, so `readRunnerDurationMs` now returns `fallbackMs` for input `"0"` instead of `0`. The only consumers are the module-level env knobs at src/shared/runner-process.ts:3 (`NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS`, default 5000) and src/shared/runner-process.ts:7 (`NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS`, default 2000), which feed the kill timers at src/shared/runner-process.ts:123-124. An operator who previously set either knob to 0 to skip the SIGTERM→SIGKILL grace (or to stop waiting immediately after SIGKILL) now silently gets a 5000 ms / 2000 ms wait instead; nothing logs or distinguishes the coerced `0` from an unset/empty value, so the previously valid config is discarded without any signal. The prior `>= 0` explicitly accepted 0, so this is a behavior change for an existing configuration rather than a non-numeric-input fallback.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop for changed files left out of hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed block (base src/core/review.ts:98-110) mapped every changed file not present in a selected hotspot into a tail hotspot so it was still deep-reviewed ("never silently skip a changed file"). HEAD selects only sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) and iterates those hotspots directly (line 97), so any changedFile the map pass does not assign to a survived hotspot - and every file in a hotspot dropped by the MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 slice - is never reviewed and never surfaced in checked/findings. A PR can therefore merge with files that the review tool silently never looked at.

findings.title: Propagate deep-review residual risks into the merged candidate
findings.whyItBreaks: HEAD hardcodes residual_risks: [] on candidateMerged and never reads res.residual_risks from each deep pass (the removed residuals.push(...) at base:127). The critic only ever sees candidateMerged, and the returned ReviewResult.residualRisks comes from pruned.residual_risks (line 128), so any residual risk a deep pass reports - including the block:true signal that base used for failures - can never reach the critic or the final result. This is silent loss of a risk/blocks signal on a changed path.

findings.title: Keep per-hotspot deep-pass failures from aborting the review
findings.whyItBreaks: Base wrapped the deep call in try/catch (base:123-132), recording a checked note and a block:true residual risk so one hotspot failure still produced a blocked-but-usable review. HEAD calls normalizeReview(extractJson(runCodex(...))) unguarded inside the hotspot loop, so any malformed/empty LLM output (extractJson throws) or runCodex error for one of up to 6 hotspots rejects the entire reviewLarge instead of returning a result - the failure reason is also no longer captured in checked. One transient hotspot failure now loses the whole review.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes in formatDuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from the raw ms while seconds are independently Math.round'ed from the remainder, so a remainder that rounds up to 60 is never carried. formatDuration(59999) -> minutes=floor(59999/60000)=0, seconds=round(59.999)=60 -> "60s" (old code: round(59.999)=60 total seconds -> minutes=1 -> "1m 0s"). Likewise formatDuration(119999) -> "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". Any duration with (ms % 60000) >= 59500 now renders a 60-second field, a user-visible regression in the stats line rendered at src/shared/render.ts:75 and src/shared/render.ts:80.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicting its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `0` is no longer rejected even though the function name (`parsePositiveInteger`), the exported signature, and the thrown message ("requires a positive integer") all promise strict positivity. Because the value is produced by `Number(value)`, this also newly admits empty/whitespace strings (`Number('') === 0`), which previously threw. Any caller relying on the promised invariant (e.g. using the result as an attempt count, size, or divisor) now receives 0 where a positive value was guaranteed, enabling a wrong/zero path that the old guard prevented. There are no in-repo callers (rg finds only the definition), but the function is exported, so the promise itself is the public contract and the validation the caller receives is weakened.
